description: I am thecreator, passionate about remote sensing and Earth sciences. My project uses NISAR radar data to detect and visualize changes on the Earth's surface: ground deformation, flooding, and water body variation. I am creating an interactive, easy-to-understand app capable of analyzing different places around the world.
summary: Qaway ("the one who watches" in Quechua) is a voice-first, mobile-optimized web app that turns NISAR (NASA-ISRO) satellite radar into spoken hazard alerts for Peru's Andean and jungle roads. Designed for the driver's phone, it lets you ask a question out loud and, hands-free, an AI agent decides which radar analysis to run and answers by voice in Spanish or English. From NISAR data it detects three life-threatening surface changes: past landslides (surface change), slow slope movement as an early warning (millimeters of ground motion before collapse), and river flooding. It uses established methods (ASF/NASA change detection with Wishart, InSAR deformation, and the NASA ARSET flood method), plus Copernicus DEM and OpenStreetMap. A second mode gives technical analysts a rigorous statistics dashboard. This addresses the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by turning complex SAR data into clear, actionable warnings. It matters because Andean and jungle roads suffer deadly landslides and floods with little warning, and Qaway lets drivers, rural communities, and authorities see danger before it strikes.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Qaway ("the one who watches" in Quechua) is an early-warning geodynamic monitoring platform that transforms raw satellite radar data from NISAR (NASA–ISRO) into immediate, actionable road-hazard alerts delivered through voice and visual analytics.

The system operates through an automated, end-to-end processing pipeline:

Geographic area capture: In driver mode, the application captures the vehicle’s live GPS position and dynamically projects a road-corridor safety buffer using OpenStreetMap and Turf.js; in analyst mode, the user manually draws a polygon over an unstable hillside or critical infrastructure.

On-demand satellite querying: The backend automatically queries NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) Search API to retrieve the latest NISAR radar granules (GCOV and GUNW) along with the Copernicus GLO-30 Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for the selected bounding box.

Scientific SAR signal processing: The core Python engine executes three quantitative physical analyses: L-band backscatter change detection (Log-Ratio dB and Wishart/Conradsen polarimetric test) to map fresh landslide scars; interferometric phase analysis (InSAR) to measure ground displacement rates in millimeters per week; and bimodal adaptive thresholding (Otsu method, validated by NASA ARSET) to detect floodwaters covering the roadway.

Tailored delivery: An agentic AI layer (powered by Gemini API or local open models with tool-calling) evaluates the resulting physical metrics against slope-stability matrices, delivering a concise, hands-free spoken warning to the driver or a comprehensive statistical dashboard to the technical analyst.

What benefits does it have?

All-weather visibility regardless of cloud cover: Unlike traditional optical satellites (such as Sentinel-2 or Landsat) which are rendered ineffective by the heavy cloud decks, torrential rainfall, and persistent fog of the Andes and Amazon basin, NISAR’s L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) penetrates clouds and operates seamlessly day and night.

Democratization of complex Earth observation data: It removes technical barriers. Truck drivers, local authorities, and residents do not need remote-sensing degrees to interpret raw HDF5 files, complex interferograms, or decibel matrices; they receive clear, actionable answers in plain, natural language.

Driver safety (Zero visual distraction): Drivers can query live road conditions without taking their hands off the wheel or their eyes off the road, interacting entirely through voice on dangerous mountain passes.

Proactive pre-collapse detection: Conventional disaster platforms only report landslides after roads are already blocked. Qaway detects slow, millimeter-scale slope deformation weeks before catastrophic failure occurs, shifting disaster management from reactive to proactive.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Saving lives on high-risk corridors: Prevents passenger buses, emergency vehicles, and cargo trucks from being buried or stranded while driving through active slope-failure zones during night hours or severe storms.

Securing logistics and vital supply chains: Along strategic arteries such as Peru’s Federico Basadre Highway (PE-5N), road closures sever fuel, food, and medical supplies between entire administrative regions (e.g., Huánuco and Pucallpa). Early detection enables carriers and public officials to divert convoys or schedule safe transit windows before supply lines break.

Optimizing public expenditure in emergency response: Provides transportation agencies (such as Provías Nacional or transport ministries) with prioritized intelligence to pre-deploy heavy earthmoving machinery to verified, moving slopes before collapse, drastically reducing emergency clearing and infrastructure rebuilding costs.

Global scalability: While validated along the steep corridors of the Peruvian Andes, Qaway’s processing pipeline is globally applicable to any mountainous or flood-prone road network covered by the NISAR constellation.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Architecture & System Design: Attribute-Driven Design (ADD) methodology to design the system architecture, structuring components around quality drivers: modularity to plug in new SAR hazard algorithms, performance for rapid processing, and fault tolerance.

Satellite & Geospatial Data: NASA–ISRO NISAR GCOV (backscatter) and GUNW (InSAR) products accessed via the ASF Search API for hazard detection; Copernicus GLO-30 DEM for slope calculation; OpenStreetMap (Overpass API) to dynamically extract road corridor geometries.

Backend & Languages: Python 3.11 with FastAPI and Uvicorn to build the asynchronous REST API that orchestrates on-demand satellite downloads and processing jobs.

Scientific SAR Processing: NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and H5py to read raw HDF5 NISAR granules, calculate backscatter change ratios, unwrap InSAR deformation phases, and execute Otsu flood thresholding; Shapely and Pyproj for spatial clipping and coordinate reprojections.

Artificial Intelligence Core: Tool-calling agent architecture utilizing the Google Gemini API (cloud inference) and local Qwen 2.5 (via Ollama accelerated on an NVIDIA RTX GPU) to interpret user intent, trigger the scientific SAR tools, and assess risk levels.

Frontend & Voice UI: HTML5, JavaScript (ES6+), and MapLibre GL JS for interactive GIS map rendering; browser-native Web Speech API for hands-free speech-to-text input and text-to-speech audio alerts.

Deployment & Infrastructure: Docker and Docker Compose for containerization, Nginx as a reverse proxy, and Cloudflare Tunnel for secure public web access.

How is your project creative?

A "Voice-first" paradigm for spaceborne radar: Remote sensing has historically been screen-bound and restricted to specialists analyzing complex GIS dashboards. Qaway inverts this paradigm by transforming raw radar data into a conversational co-pilot that talks directly to drivers in transit.

Agentic AI with autonomous scientific reasoning: Rather than relying on a static chatbot or rigid dropdown menus, the system employs an agent that interprets user intent, autonomously decides which scientific radar algorithm to execute (landslide change detection, InSAR creep, or flood mapping), evaluates multi-factor hazard thresholds, and tailors its output tone (plain speech for drivers vs. quantitative statistics for engineers).

Culturally grounded, empathetic design: The system humanizes space technology through Qaway, an animated Andean llama adorned in a traditional Peruvian blanket who surveys the road. This culturally rooted design breaks down intimidation toward high-tech science and builds trust among rural drivers and local communities.

What factors did your team consider?

In-transit driver safety and ergonomics: Mitigating cognitive load and visual distraction was non-negotiable. On narrow, cliffside Andean roads with hairpin turns, mud, and zero-visibility fog, requiring a driver to inspect a phone screen is dangerous; hands-free voice was the only viable channel.

Extreme topography and meteorological realities: Tropical cloud forests and steep Andean slopes experience torrential rains and near-continuous cloud cover throughout the wet season. This ruled out optical imagery and made L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) indispensable.

Regional coverage gaps in global products: Our team identified that preprocessed displacement services like OPERA DISP only cover North America down to Panama, leaving South America uncovered. Qaway was deliberately architected to process raw NISAR GUNW interferograms directly, ensuring full coverage for Peru and the wider Andean region.

Low-bandwidth cellular environments: Remote rural highways frequently suffer from spotty mobile connectivity. The system optimizes network efficiency by clipping radar granules on the server to the exact road buffer and transmitting lightweight text and synthesized voice responses to the client.

AI Tools Used

- Qwen 2.5 (via Ollama) — core product feature: the in-app voice agent is a local LLM using tool-calling to decide which NISAR analysis to run and to narrate the result to the driver.

- Google Gemini API — alternative LLM provider for the same agent, so it can run serverless / without a GPU.

- Claude (Claude Code, Anthropic) — development support: coding, debugging, cloud-deployment setup, and drafting/editing documentation and this write-up.
